papers.title: Interference-Aware Tone Selection for Bluetooth Channel Sounding
papers.summary: Bluetooth Channel Sounding enables distance estimation using phase measurements across multiple frequencies. However, coexistence with Wi-Fi and other 2.4 GHz radios can fragment the available frequency band, making reliable ranging difficult when only a limited number of tones can be selected. Drawing on sparse antenna-array theory, we show that interference avoidance alone is insufficient: the spacing of selected tones can introduce repeated peaks in the ranging response, leading to estimation errors. We propose a lightweight, interference-aware tone-selection method that jointly considers frequency occupancy, tone spacing, and frequency span. Our method constructs a 15-tone map using a three-step rule without ranging measurements, ground-truth distance, or online candidate-map search. We evaluate the method using simulations of 900 indoor environments, a public Bluetooth Channel Sounding dataset, and measurements from commercial Nordic nRF54L15 hardware. Compared with random interference avoiding baseline, our proposed method improves ranging success percentage by 39 points under mixed interference, 29 points on the public dataset, and 82 points in hardware experiments. These results demonstrate the importance of tone selection for practical Bluetooth Channel Sounding.

papers.title: DexAttention: Distributed Sparse Attention through Rapid Online Planning and Persistent GPU Execution
papers.summary: Sparse attention reduces computation, but distributed execution may still transfer unnecessary data and incur substantial per-operation overhead. Mask-aware assignment and scheduling can reduce these costs, but replanning for dynamic masks must be cheaper than the execution time it saves. We present DexAttention, a distributed sparse attention system that co-designs fast online planning with persistent execution. Its assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance computational load and reduce communication. A lightweight greedy scheduler orders coarse communication and computation operations, while a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready tasks. This division keeps detailed synchronization out of planning while enabling overlap without repeated attention launches. The framework supports static and dynamic per-head masks across multiple attention compute kernels. On a four-node, 16-GPU cluster, DexAttention achieves a $1.39\times$ geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations. For dynamic video attention, it achieves $2.11$--$2.37\times$ speedups over Ring Attention including planning.

papers.title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
papers.summary: Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity. We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds---a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan---enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

papers.title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving
papers.summary: As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput.

papers.title: Detecting Empty Abstractions and Pruning Dead Paths in the Linux eBPF Verifier with Abstract Step Functions
papers.summary: The Linux kernel's eBPF verifier uses abstract interpretation to ensure the safety of user-provided programs before execution. It tracks each register with multiple interval domains and a bitwise domain (tristate numbers). Refining the abstract state at conditional branches can produce mutually contradictory constraints across domains, indicating an unreachable path. However, the verifier lacks an empty-set ($\bot$) representation and cannot detect when these domains have an empty intersection, causing it to analyze dead paths. Passing such contradictory states into domain reduction or downstream operators violates their implicit non-emptiness precondition, triggering domain invariant violations. This has been a multi-year issue in the Linux kernel causing production outages, false rejections, and state explosion. This paper presents a sound and complete constant-time emptiness check across the eBPF verifier's abstract domains to prune dead branches. We introduce abstract step functions, a general framework that tests whether intervals and non-convex domains intersect in O(1) time without scanning individual values. We develop tnum_step, a formally verified constant-time operator that jumps to the next integer satisfying a tristate bitmask. Using tnum_step, we design a multi-domain emptiness check that detects contradictory states during branch refinement and immediately prunes unreachable branches, eliminating the root cause of dead-branch invariant violations. Our technique prevents invariant violations, state explosion, and false rejections while incurring negligible (1.48%) overhead across Linux kernel selftests and production suites such as Cilium. Our tnum_step operator has been upstreamed into the mainline Linux kernel.

papers.title: Polymorph: Operating System Kernel Optimization Through Artificial Intelligence
papers.summary: While popular operating systems such as Linux and Windows were originally designed as monolithic kernels, an increasing number of kernel subsystems have become extensible using eBPF. Users can now define custom policies for essential kernel mechanisms, such as the process scheduler, page cache, and network stack, without recompiling the kernel. These mechanisms give developers significant freedom to fit the kernel to their applications' workloads, but the question of which policy to deploy remains open. We study how to use agentic AI to automate kernel policy development, selection, and deployment, focusing on the page cache and the process scheduler as two representative subsystems. We show that existing approaches fall short: evolutionary and agentic search runs offline, is relatively expensive, and often fails to generalize to online workloads, while online knob tuners are encumbered by the knobs' lack of expressivity. In contrast, we propose Polymorph, which learns online: an AI agent writes a generalized, granular policy once, and a user mode tuner adjusts its parameters during runtime, with no LLM in the loop. For the page cache, Polymorph improves throughput over Linux's LRU by 8.4% on unseen data, nearly twice the gain of the best existing policy, while adapting to workload changes at runtime and costing only 16M tokens once, versus 125-240M tokens per workload for agentic offline search. For the process scheduler, it improves on Linux's default by 2.75x across six workloads, versus 2.27x for the best fixed sched_ext policy.

papers.title: Benchmarking Linux CGroup and Schedule Idle
papers.summary: cgroups are a Linux kernel primitive that limits, accounts for, and isolates the resource usage (CPU, memory, disk I/O) of a collection of processes. Many provider-side serverless systems (Mitosis, gVisor, Havest VM, FAASM) leverage linux containers based around cgroups/namespaces for their performance isolation. However, how well does this primitive map to the needs of serverless platforms? How does the linux CFS scheduler deal with cgroups and SCHED IDLE and what are the core sources of high tail latency? Would a new primitive design fit the needs of serverless isolation better? In this work we take the first step to answering these questions by profiling the current behavior of cgroups and a sched idle policy via a thorough benchmarking study. We emulate the setting of Performance-Critical (LC) server in the presence of an intensive background (BE) process and note the impact of each primitive on the performance of the server. We show it is non-trivial to balance the potential tail-latency impact on a LC server with the throughput of BE tasks. Furthermore, there are many variables to adjust for the developer between hard maximum bandwidth limits, weighted cpu shares, the presence of the sched idle policy, or additionally "niceness" priority in the scheduling policy.

papers.title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
papers.summary: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.

papers.title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation
papers.summary: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.

papers.title: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy
papers.summary: Many distributed systems achieve high performance by relying on dedicated sequencers to order requests, leaving replicas to commit them in that order. Despite more than a decade of such sequencer-aided coordination (SAC) systems, from Corfu and NOPaxos to LazyLog and SwitchBFT, their correctness has been argued only with pen-and-paper proofs or bounded model checking at the protocol level. In this paper, we formally verify implementations of SAC protocols. The sequencer seems to make this easy: it decides the order of all requests, so the proof can place each request's linearization point at the sequencer using a well-known technique, prophecy variables. Yet a linearization point placed at the sequencer is not durable, because the sequencer orders a request before any replica commits it. Crashes and other rare events may trigger a view change that discards the request, nullifying the earlier decision and the proof that rests on it. Our framework, Stephen, extends prophecy variables to handle view changes, and we make three contributions. (1) We develop cross-view prophecy peek, which lets the proof follow a request across view changes until it is either committed or permanently discarded. (2) Our verification uncovered bugs in existing SAC implementations, including one that can lose committed requests. We fix them and prove the fixes correct. (3) We apply Stephen to NOPaxos, Corfu and LazyLog. We build verified implementations with machine-checked proofs of linearizability. They perform within 17% of their open-source, unverified counterparts. The verified implementations and proofs will be open-sourced.

papers.title: Capability Internet: A Network Architecture for Autonomous Agents
papers.summary: Autonomous agents increasingly provide and consume network services. An agent coordinating a long-running task across organizations must track what has been done, which actions are authorized, and which provider can perform the next step. We propose Capability Internet (CI), an architecture in which agents exchange capabilities and coordinate their use through persistent tasks. Versioned descriptions specify behavior, and live instances identify the providers and resources that can supply it. Task records link each invocation to its selected instance, authority, and terms of use. When providers change, the task can reuse completed results that still meet its requirements. Five functions support capability discovery, task coordination, federated compute, intelligence reuse, and governance of capability use and settlement. Reviewed task results can supply versioned intelligence for subsequent tasks. We illustrate CI through four deployment profiles covering computing and intelligence services, manufacturing, vehicles and embodied robots, and space-ground operations, and propose an evaluation plan.

papers.title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
papers.summary: Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations. We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.

papers.title: Neural Memory Orchestration
papers.summary: Modern HPC workloads increasingly stall on the memory hierarchy rather than on compute, and page faults from mmap'd files, swap, and tiered memory are a growing fraction of wall time. Heuristic prefetchers in the kernel handle stride-like and temporally clustered patterns well but degrade sharply on the irregular, data-dependent access streams typical of these workloads. Learned prefetchers have been shown to capture such patterns in simulation but have not been taken to a deployed pipeline running against live workloads on real hardware. We present Overseer, an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system. An eBPF collector observes page faults on the target host, a transformer predictor (OverNet) runs on network-attached inference hardware and emits future page addresses, and a kernel-resident enforcer materializes those pages into the target's address space before they are demanded. OverNet encodes fault sequences through per-instance ordinal ranks over deltas, which lets a single trained model serve any target process without retraining. On two page-fault-heavy workloads, Overseer reduces runtime by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication, with corresponding reductions in major-fault counts.

papers.title: HETEROVLM: Edge Multi-Request Vision-Language Model Serving on a Heterogeneous Versal SoC with AI Engines and Programmable Logic
papers.summary: Edge devices in vehicles and robots serve concurrent requests with different deadlines to a vision-language model (VLM), each mixing a compute-bound encoder and prefill with a memory-bound decode. GPU serving targets datacenter throughput with per-iteration host scheduling: an urgent request waits for the running iteration, and small-batch decode costs much energy per token. Prior accelerators on Versal AI Engine (AIE) SoCs map one model onto a fixed AIE dataflow graph for one input stream, without decode or request scheduling. HETEROVLM keeps the AIE graph static and makes it schedulable. The AIE array runs the encoder, prefill and attention, and the programmable logic (PL) holds GEMV engines for small decode steps and a scheduler that orders short work units by class and deadline. Concurrent requests share one decode step that reads the weights once. An urgent request preempts at a work-unit boundary, and the paused request resumes from its results in DDR. On an AMD Versal VC1902, text and camera questions get their first tokens in 140 and 303 ms. HETEROVLM decodes a single request 1.3x and 4.0x faster than NVIDIA Tesla T4 and Jetson Orin Nano GPUs, with 61% and 73% of their energy per token, and uses 51% of the energy per token of an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 Ti. The same bitstream serves multiple VLMs by loading their own instruction programs and weights. A demo is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/demo heterovlm-EFM2/.

papers.title: Locality-Aware Scheduling for Stream Processing Applications in Serverless Environments
papers.summary: Stateful Serverless (Function-as-a-Service) environment are increasingly used for stream processing applications. These applications are often structured as pipelines where data flows through a sequence of distinct processing operators. Many operators are stateful and require access to the processing state during execution. To address this, stateful serverless platforms introduce state servers on worker nodes, co-locating state with computation to dramatically reduce access latency. In serverless, these data pipelines are realized by chaining function invocations, passing the processed data from one function to the next. To reduce network overhead, state-of-the-art scheduling approaches employ a distributed worker-level scheduling model, routing locally generated chained requests directly to destination workers, bypassing centralized schedulers. However, these approaches always co-locate state and execution for the same operator in the same worker, which forces most invocations to the next operator to be transferred across workers, thereby increasing both latency and I/O overhead. As a result, this paper proposes LcSched, a novel distributed scheduling strategy tailored for stream processing applications in stateful serverless environments. LcSched seeks to maximise local execution of chained function invocations while ensuring that each execution accesses its state from the local worker. It also monitors workload at runtime to maintain workload balance between workers. Experimental results show that LcSched improves throughput by up to 3.6x and reduces end-to-end latency by up to 79% compared to the state-of-the-art distributed scheduling strategy for stateful serverless environments.

papers.title: Accelerating Distributed Digital Ising Machines
papers.summary: Ising machines, dedicated accelerators built around the dynamics of Ising-like spin models, have emerged as a leading platform for combinatorial optimization and probabilistic sampling. The problems that motivate them require millions of spins, far beyond the on-chip capacity of any single device, so a practical Ising machine must distribute its computation across many devices. Prior work reports throughput at a single operating point, leaving the binding resource unidentified and platform crossovers measurable only by experiment; no calibrated cross-platform cost model of distributed Ising machines has been reported, nor have systematic techniques to accelerate their Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workloads. This work presents a calibrated cost model that decomposes digital Ising sweep time into compute, memory, synchronization, and inter-device communication terms, validated with 4.8% mean error across three GPU generations, FPGA and ASIC up to 1 million spins. Guided by the model, we address each term in turn and propose: (i) a data placement strategy, worth up to 4.2$\times$ speedup; (ii) multi-rate and bounded-staleness schedules that relax the barrier that Gibbs sampling imposes, cutting time-to-solution (TTS) by up to 3.16$\times$ on three benchmarks; and (iii) a phase-offset streaming dataflow that hides boundary exchange behind interior computation whenever a link satisfies a latency-transparency criterion, yielding up to 1.25$\times$/1.74$\times$/2.01$\times$ on an H200 pair, a ZCU106 pair, and a four-board XEM8320 $2{\times}2$ mesh. The streaming dataflow is also implemented on a fabricated four-chip 28 nm ASIC sustaining 28.1 Gflips/s at 4.81 pJ/flip.

papers.title: Inference-Time Scaling in Agentic Hardware Verification Workflows: A Multi-Strategy Characterization Across Protocol Complexity
papers.summary: Inference-time scaling, allocating more compute during generation rather than pre-training, has demonstrated dramatic quality improvements for LLM reasoning tasks. Its behaviour in structured hardware verification code generation, where outputs must satisfy compiler correctness, protocol semantics, and functional coverage constraints simultaneously, is less understood. We present a systematic, simulator-grounded study of inference-time compute scaling for agentic UVM testbench synthesis targeting AMBA protocol bridges. Four inference strategies---zero-shot (\$0.04), raw-feedback iterative (\$0.81), structured inner-loop (\$0.95), and full dual-loop agentic synthesis (\$1.06)---are evaluated across four AMBA targets (Protocol Complexity Index 11.8--22.6) using the Protocol Verification Completeness (PVC) metric, functional coverage, and a six-class UVM error taxonomy (E1--E6). Our central finding is that structured diagnostic feedback acts as an inference-time compute multiplier: the structured inner loop yields roughly $15\times$ more PVC per inference dollar than raw EDA-tool feedback (marginal efficiency, S1$\to$S2 vs. S0$\to$S1). The mechanism is fault targeting, not token reduction: raw compiler feedback drives the testbench to compile but cannot surface functional protocol faults that leave the code syntactically valid, whereas structured E1--E6 bundles diagnose and resolve them. All outputs are judged by a cycle-accurate Mentor Questa toolchain rather than by model self-assessment; the dual-loop strategy reaches PVC $\geq$ 0.95 with zero scoreboard errors on every target, and the generated environments surfaced a latent RTL bug in two of the four reference designs. These results establish a principled compute-quality trade-off curve for LLM-aided verification environment generation and motivate inference-budget-aware deployment strategies for industrial EDA workflows.

papers.title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation
papers.summary: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.

papers.title: ReCIM-HD: A 40 nm On-Device Learning Accelerator with Hyperdimensional Computing via Importance-Based Hybrid Digital-ReRAM CIM
papers.summary: ReCIM-HD is an on-device learning (ODL) accelerator that integrates gradient-free hyperdimensional computing (HDC) with resistive RAM (ReRAM)-based analog compute-in-memory (CIM). ReCIM-HD introduces three key techniques: (1) ultra-low-power HDC-based edge ODL without costly back-propagation operations; (2) non-volatile ReRAM-based storage for class hypervectors and CIM similarity search, enabling energy-efficient inference and power-gating during idle periods without data loss; and (3) a hybrid digital-analog CIM inference flow that protects a small accuracy-critical subset digitally to preserve accuracy. Additionally, it employs a Kronecker HD encoder (KE) to reduce encoding overhead and a customized instruction set architecture (ISA) to support flexible programmability. Fabricated in 40 nm, ReCIM-HD achieves 44.17 TOPS/W (hybrid mode) and 75.8 TOPS/W (ReRAM CIM mode), delivering up to 20.1x higher energy efficiency than the state-of-the-art accelerator.

papers.title: Continuum: Boundary-State-Aware Deterministic Scheduling in Dynamic LEO Networks
papers.summary: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations support mission-critical services requiring bounded latency and predictable delivery. However, conventional snapshot-based schedulers discard the forwarding progress of unfinished time-triggered traffic across topology transitions, degrading schedulability and timing consistency. We present Continuum, aboundary-state-aware rolling-horizon scheduling framework. Continuum inherits buffered-node and arrival-time information, jointly optimizing remaining routes and transmission slots, and refines latency to improve timing consistency while preserving original timing constraints. Ablations show up to 16.6 percentage points higher schedulability from boundary-state inheritance and a 10.9-37.7 times reduction in mean jitter from joint alignment. Scalability experiments evaluate synthesis performance for workloads of up to 10K flows.

papers.title: LEDGE: An Efficient Simulator for Distributed LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
papers.summary: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. An efficient simulator for edge LLM serving must support diverse, fine-grained placement configurations, capture runtime behavior, and accurately predict execution times while keeping simulation overhead low. We present LEDGE, a lightweight simulator for fast, fine-grained evaluation of distributed LLM serving on heterogeneous edge devices without executing tensor operations. LEDGE constructs event graphs supporting non-uniform tensor and pipeline parallelism, estimates execution costs using reusable performance models calibrated from end-to-end measurements, and simulates shared-link contention. We evaluate LEDGE on a heterogeneous testbed of 10 Jetson and Raspberry Pi devices, covering 17 model--precision combinations across 4 LLM families. On Qwen deployments, LEDGE achieves request-level mean absolute percentage errors below 3.6% and a 135.3 times aggregate speedup over physical inference. Performance model calibrated on one LLM family yield 7.44% zero-shot end-to-end latency MAPE across three other families. Further simulations show how shared-link contention affects placement decisions and network topology constrains scaling. Across four edge environments, LEDGE completes 26,773 simulation runs in 83.8 minutes, enabling efficient exploration of deployment strategies under diverse resource conditions and serving objectives. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/gdfwj/LEDGE.

papers.title: eFAIR: Fair LLM Serving under Hourly Electricity Commitments
papers.summary: Datacenters can procure electricity in day-ahead markets by committing to energy purchases for individual hours. For LLM services operating within these hourly budgets, maximizing aggregate throughput alone may still leave individual requests waiting or receiving much slower service than desired. Fair serving therefore requires improving service for poorly served requests while reserving electricity for later arrivals whose timing and demand are unknown. To compare service across requests, we define normalized throughput as each request's actual output rate divided by the product of its standalone throughput and its service entitlement, a positive weight representing its desired service level. Using this measure, we formulate fair serving as leximin optimization under an hourly electricity constraint, prioritizing requests with the lowest normalized throughput. To address this problem, we present eFAIR, an online scheduler that coordinates request dispatching, electricity budget allocation, and GPU frequency selection through a common normalized-throughput target. Specifically, request dispatching prioritizes requests by desired service level and progress; electricity budget allocation reserves electricity for current and expected future work; and frequency selection uses electricity savings to raise GPU frequencies for requests with higher desired service levels. Evaluations on H20 and H200 configurations, each with 32 replicas, show that eFAIR improves the tenth percentile of normalized throughput by 28.0%-31.0% over the best budget-feasible baseline, while keeping absolute deviations from the hourly electricity commitment below 0.26%. eFAIR also improves throughput balance among concurrent requests and aligns electricity allocation more closely with service demand over time. Together, these results demonstrate how eFAIR improves request-level fairness within an hourly commitment.

papers.title: Conditional What-If Generation for Radio Access Network Energy under Rare and Unseen Contexts
papers.summary: Energy-saving mechanisms in RANs must balance energy reduction and network performance under varying traffic conditions. Conditional generative models support what-if analysis by generating plausible power-consumption trajectories for radio configurations and operating scenarios, helping operators evaluate energy-saving policies before deployment. However, representative measurements are costly and operationally constrained, so historical data cover only limited configurations and conditions, leaving some contexts poorly represented or unseen during training. In this paper, we study conditional generation of RAN power-consumption trajectories under decreasing training coverage, from well-represented to rare and unseen configurations. We first introduce a context-normalized conditional generator combining temporally aligned conditioning with configuration-dependent target normalization. It improves generation for well-represented configurations but becomes less reliable as training exposure decreases because target consumption is harder to estimate. We therefore introduce a prediction-based generative framework that decomposes power consumption into global prediction, residual level and scale correction, and temporal residual generation. Experiments on a commercial 5G RAN and a public dataset show that hardware metadata provides transferable information about residual scale, while limited target observations at inference improve generation through residual-level correction without retraining. An ablation study confirms that residual-level correction provides most of the gain. Both approaches outperform state-of-the-art methods for well-represented configurations, while the prediction-based approach also generalizes to rare and unseen contexts and, with one target observation, reduces median MAE by about 50% compared with TimeWeaver.

papers.title: Hardware Acceleration of Vision-Language-Action Models with Weight Precision Rising over the Flow Steps
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as GR00T control robots through an action head: a diffusion transformer that turns noise into a chunk of actions in a few flow-matching steps. Every step re-reads all of the head's weights from DRAM but applies each weight to only about fifty tokens. Inference is therefore memory-bound, and its latency and energy are largely determined by the total number of transferred weight bits. We show that later flow steps attenuate the quantization errors of earlier steps, so the weight precision of an action head should rise over the steps. With plain per-channel rounding and without calibration or training, widths rising over the steps from 2 to 4 bits preserve the closed-loop success of robot policies. These widths transfer 25% fewer bits than 4-bit weights at every step. However, we show that on Jetson AGX Thor, current GPU kernels cannot exploit this per-step precision due to fixed overheads. We therefore present a programmable accelerator whose latency and energy both scale with the transferred weight bits. It decodes entropy-coded weights for bit-serial sub-arrays at the DRAM rate. Because the width changes per step, a run-time allocator divides these sub-arrays between the linear layers and the attention to balance their workloads. The same sub-arrays are thus capable of running action heads of different families and sizes, as well as a vision-language model. On the DRAM side, a requantizer and an entropy encoder at each bank let one stored 8-bit copy replace the copies of all widths. Simulated with LPDDR5X timing, our RTL implementation runs the GR00T N1.6 action head in 8.02 ms per inference with 2, 3, 3 and 4 bits in its four flow steps. With a copy per width and 50% of Thor's memory bandwidth, the accelerator runs this schedule 1.7x faster than Thor in NVFP4, at 9.1x less energy and equal closed-loop success.

papers.title: Multilevel Graph Partitioning on GPU Supercomputers
papers.summary: Graph partitioning is a key enabler in computational science, with applications to sparse linear algebra, load-balanced parallel computation, and graph computations. In recent years, graphics processing units (GPUs) have become the preferred accelerator on the world's top supercomputers. Despite this, most existing distributed graph partitioners do not utilize GPUs. In this work, we develop a new multi-GPU distributed partitioner based on Jet, a prior single-GPU partitioner. We seek to optimize scalability without sacrificing quality. Our partitioner utilizes CUDA-aware MPI, one-sided communication routines, and an overall bulk-synchronous parallel structure. We demonstrate solution quality comparable to Jet. Our experiments show excellent weak scaling up to 256 GPUs, enabling partitioning of instances significantly larger than a single-GPU partitioner can handle.

papers.title: ScaleBench: An Extensible and Reproducible Experimental Platform for Kubernetes Autoscaling Research
papers.summary: Autoscaling enables cloud-native applications to meet their SLOs by dynamically adjusting computational resources at runtime. Recent research has explored a broad range of advanced autoscaling approaches, including rule-based, optimisation-based, and machine learning-based techniques, to address the limitations of traditional resource management strategies in cloud-native environments. Despite significant advances, a considerable gap remains between academic innovations and their practical adoption in real-world environments. For instance, Kubernetes deployments commonly rely on the reactive, CPU-based Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, limiting the adoption of more advanced autoscaling approaches. Recent studies have investigated challenges such as autoscaler configuration and reproducible performance evaluation; however, the practical deployment, integration complexity, and operational overhead of research-based autoscalers in Kubernetes environments have received limited attention. To address this gap, we present ScaleBench, a native Kubernetes experimental platform to enable extensible and reproducible evaluation of autoscaling solutions. Unlike existing approaches, ScaleBench integrates autoscalers as native Kubernetes components, allowing researchers to assess not only scaling performance but also deployment characteristics and integration requirements within realistic cloud-native environments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ScaleBench by evaluating multiple autoscaling approaches through a case study. The results highlight its capability to support systematic, repeatable, and practical assessment of Kubernetes autoscaling approaches.

papers.title: Dissecting an Unexplored SASS Control-Code Field: Barrier Exemption and Programmable Warp Priority
papers.summary: Every instruction in NVIDIA's native GPU ISA (SASS) carries a control code that guides hardware scheduling, and prior work has decoded its known fields to optimize GPU kernels. However, one control-code field remains unexplored: it appears over 500000 times in NVIDIA's closed-source libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN, yet nvcc never emits it when compiling user programs. This paper presents the first systematic study of this control-code field across GPU architectures from Volta to Blackwell. Using instruction-level microbenchmarks, we show that the field controls two independent hardware mechanisms: barrier exemption (EXEMPT), which allows instructions blocked by a pending barrier to issue early during the barrier wait, and programmable warp priority (START, TILE, and END), which moves warps across three priority levels in the hardware scheduler. We identify the conditions under which each mechanism improves GPU kernel performance and implement a post-compilation binary optimizer that places these marks directly in compiled binaries without modifying source code or the compiler. Evaluated across six GPUs spanning four architectures, our optimizations speed up representative kernels by up to 31.9%, and the optimizer accelerates production kernels in llama.cpp and vLLM by up to 5.4% and end-to-end LLM inference by up to 3.6%.

papers.title: A Runtime System for Mitigating Crossbar Port Contention on SM-Partitioned GPUs
papers.summary: To avoid scheduling delays when running concurrent workloads on a GPU, Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning mechanisms such as CUDA Green Contexts restrict each workload to separate SMs. Despite this partitioning, concurrent workloads still significantly slow down latency-critical workloads, which recent studies attribute to shared L2 cache and memory contention. However, contention also occurs at the crossbar ports connecting each Graphics Processing Cluster (GPC) of SMs to the L2 cache, as all SMs in a GPC share one port. Green Contexts spread workloads across GPCs, placing concurrent workloads in the same GPCs and forcing latency-critical memory requests to queue behind background requests. Packing workloads into separate GPCs avoids this contention, but forces latency-critical memory requests through fewer ports, limiting memory bandwidth. Consequently, neither spreading nor packing is always faster across workloads and GPUs. Based on these observations, we present GPCPlace, a runtime system that dynamically selects between spreading and packing by profiling workloads on the target GPU to estimate both slowdowns, and hooks kernel launches in the CUDA driver to set SM masks without application modifications. Across 14 GPUs and 112 workload cases, GPCPlace speeds up latency-critical workloads by up to 1.15x on average and 2.38x maximum over Green Contexts without degrading throughput.

papers.title: TechReport: Implementing CHERI in gem5
papers.summary: Despite countless mitigation efforts, memory safety issues still prevail. The recently discovered security issues in PHP underline this fact. One of the most promising approaches to solving this problem is the concept of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions (CHERI). There is a well-developed ecosystem of ISA simulators, compilers, operating systems, and hardware designs that support CHERI. However, the lack of a simulator modeling microarchitectural detail hinders efficient and fast design space exploration for CHERI-enhanced designs means the performance impact of CHERI remains understudied. Therefore, we present gem5-CHERI: a CHERI-enhanced adaptation of the gem5 simulator that can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads. The simulator is available open-source on GitHub.

papers.title: Cooperative UAV and Ground Station for Robust MEC of Dynamic Aquatic IoT: A Generative AI-Enhanced Approach
papers.summary: The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard to tackle. Therefore, we propose the algorithm of generative artificial intelligence-enhanced heterogeneous agent proximal policy optimization (GAI-HAPPO). The proposed algorithm integrates GAI models to enhance the actor network ability to model complex environments and extract high-level features, thereby allowing the algorithm to predict uncertainties and adapt to dynamic conditions. Additionally, GAI stabilizes the critic network, addressing the instability of multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches. Finally, extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark methods, thus highlighting the potentials in tackling intricate, cross-domain issues in the considered scenarios.

papers.title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
papers.summary: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.

papers.title: TTL Approximations for a Family of CLOCK-Like Cache Replacement Policies
papers.summary: While CLOCK-like cache replacement policies are highly appealing in practice due to their frugal memory usage and implementation simplicity, analytical models for their performance remain limited. The difficulty stems from the "eviction hand" itself. As it scans sequentially for an evictee, sparing objects with survival counters along the way, it inherently entangles the state of one cached object with the next. This strong coupling heavily obscures the system's steady state. To address this gap, we introduce a time-to-live (TTL) approximation for a family of eviction policies---which we term CLOCK($K$)---that decouples individual object dynamics using a globally fixed timer. In contrast to the intrinsic coupling induced by assuming a fixed cache capacity, such a TTL proxy yields a tractable matrix-analytic solution for the steady-state miss ratio functions across a broad and highly expressive class of phase-type renewal traffic. Among other benefits, this effectively reduces the analysis per-object to solving a linear system of order $O(Kd)$, where $d$ is the phase dimension. Moreover, our model for CLOCK($K$) recovers the canonical CLOCK when $K=1$ and FIFO when $K=0$, while empirically exhibiting Schur-concavity under the Independent Reference Model (IRM). Finally, we validate the model against a suite of trace-driven simulations.

papers.title: Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic
papers.summary: The frequent static failure of CMOS logic gates at ultra-low voltages has historically been perceived as a strict barrier to extreme voltage scaling: this paper introduces a statistical circuit law proving this intuition wrong. We discovered a universal power law connecting gate and circuit static failure probabilities, revealing that circuit failure requires the simultaneous breakdown of an entire gate cluster rather than a single component. Because the required cluster size increases rapidly as voltage drops, low-voltage \textit{sub-digital} logic exhibits surprising inherent resilience to static failure. This insight stems from new theoretical tools we developed to quantify static failure, extending well beyond conventional voltage-margin analysis. Consequently, sub-digital processors could potentially offer a viable, near-term solution to drastically reduce the energy demands of AI.

papers.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
papers.summary: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

papers.title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
papers.summary: Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent. We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides asynchrony and choreographic nondeterminism, Nyarlathotep supports expressive features including general branching, out-of-order execution, and general recursion with parameterised procedures that processes can enter independently. We prove EPP sound and complete, establishing strong behavioural equivalence between the semantics of choreographies and their projected networks. We prove that projected networks are communication-safe and deadlock-free. We mechanised all our results in Lean 4.

papers.title: Can Bandits Learn to Share a Channel? Distributed Multi-Armed Bandits for Slotted ALOHA
papers.summary: Slotted ALOHA networks constitute a playground for research on machine learning (ML)-based channel access schemes. We consider ML agents deployed in such networks and operating under severe constraints: fully distributed (independent operation), fully online (no pre-training), aperiodic (no fixed schedule), and with no explicit coordination (no signaling). We ask whether a multi-armed bandit (MAB), a minimal reinforcement learning agent, can learn the optimal policy for a capture-free slotted ALOHA system. We evaluate several MAB algorithms on aggregate network throughput and per-node fairness. Our best-performing agent is based on a Softmax bandit, which we call SALSA (Softmax ALOHA Learning for Shared Access). SALSA learns a per-node transmission policy close to optimal, with throughput near the theoretical maximum for fair random access. We achieve performance comparable to a competing state-of-the-art solution, but without requiring a priori knowledge of the network size.

papers.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
papers.summary: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

papers.title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
papers.summary: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.

papers.title: Mine Locally, Verify Globally: Exact Recovery, Compilation, and Distortion of Mined Temporal Rules
papers.summary: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces. Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes, whose clocks may not be synchronized, and events may be lost or reordered during transmission. In this paper, we study how to aggregate the coverage of mined rules across observers, determine whether their temporal windows are needed during monitoring, and characterize their detection under event loss. Our evaluation uses IPv6 packet traces collected from 21 receivers across four continents. We show that local mining followed by global confirmation recovers centralized rule coverage under suitable conditions while substantially reducing communication overhead. In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches. A window-gain criterion identifies rules that require temporal state, while our loss analysis and broker experiments demonstrate why contiguous losses can be more damaging than independent losses. The results identify separate requirements for aggregating observations, selecting monitor state, and handling event loss.

papers.title: blaris: Windowless Random-Access LZSS for Constrained Microcontrollers
papers.summary: Embedded LZ77 decompressors (such as heatshrink and tamp) require an in-RAM sliding window that couples memory usage to compression ratio and incurs high latency on random-access reads. We present blaris, a lightweight, windowless LZSS decompressor for execute-in-place (XIP) random access on constrained microcontrollers. By partitioning tokens into bidirectionally traversable streams with power-of-two checkpoints, blaris resolves back-references directly in the compressed payload, achieving compression ratios comparable to high-window heatshrink and tamp configurations without allocating a RAM window. Targeting compress-on-host, decompress-on-device workflows, blaris assumes trusted build-time payloads and omits runtime error and bounds checks. On RV32IMC, it requires just 548-784 B of Flash and 104-112 B of total RAM, achieving orders-of-magnitude faster small-slice random reads than ratio-matched, block-indexed heatshrink and tamp.

papers.title: The Obsolescence of High-Level Code: Agentic Generation from Semantic Artifacts
papers.summary: This paper argues that high-level source code need not remain the primary persistent artifact of software development when AI agents can generate, validate, and regenerate executable implementations from semantic intent. We place this claim in historical context by revisiting application generators, CASE tools, model-driven development, and platforms such as GeneXus, where developers already maintained higher-level representations from which code and other artifacts were derived. We propose a unifying view in which generation is the fundamental operation: given a semantic specification S = (R, C, I, T, O), maintained as the semantic authority, an agent produces a generated executable artifact A. Functional requirements, contracts, and interfaces are assessed as semantic obligations, while tests and operational objectives are assessed by an explicit external oracle V(A, S). We operationalize this framework through an experiment in independent generation: multiple LLVM artifacts are generated directly from one frozen semantic authority and evaluated by the same external oracle. The experiment reports regeneration coherence on an evaluated domain, not a proof of absolute correctness. It provides initial evidence that independently generated executable artifacts can produce the same observable outcomes under a common semantic authority and external oracle. We conclude by discussing reproducibility, specification-centered evolution, and the implications of treating implementation representation as a deployment choice rather than the primary maintained artifact.

papers.title: f2x50: A Repository-Scale Benchmark for Fortran-to-X Software Migration
papers.summary: Repository-level migration requires more than translating isolated functions: it must preserve behaviour across modules, shared state, build structure, and dependencies. Existing translation benchmarks predominantly cover small programs or small repositories, or fixed and widely studied language pairs. We present f2x50, a target-independent benchmark comprising 50 public Fortran repositories pinned to exact Git revisions. It contains 12,116 Git-tracked Fortran files and 6,569,806 lines, divided into three structural-complexity tiers and paired with 561 deterministic behavioural probes. Of these probes, 446 compile pinned source files with small drivers and span 131 repository--routine pairs. Every repository has at least five direct checks that collectively execute at least two routines. f2x50 provides target-independent tools for acquisition, validation, licence review, and reproducibility, together with a reference adapter for evaluating Python targets. The remaining probes are explicitly classified as extractions, inline reimplementations, or synthetic fixtures. The benchmark therefore supports comparable evaluations across migration tools and target languages.

papers.title: Plug-and-Play Sensor Evolution in Software-Defined Vehicles through Asset Administration Shells
papers.summary: Software-defined vehicles (SDVs) promise continuous software evolution, but sensor integration in deployed vehicles still depends on manual configuration, hardware-specific drivers, and repeated application-side adaptation. Existing standards address only parts of this problem. AUTOSAR standardizes selected sensor interfaces, the Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS) standardizes signal semantics, and Asset Administration Shells (AAS) standardize digital asset descriptions. However, these building blocks are rarely combined into an end-to-end onboarding path for sensors attached after vehicle deployment. This paper presents an AAS-driven plug-and-play sensor integration framework for safety-supervised sensors. Each sensor is represented by an AAS that combines hardware identification, interface metadata, VSS mappings, and references to containerized driver and optional application software. After physical connection, an edge gateway identifies the device, retrieves the matching AAS, deploys the referenced software, and publishes the resulting data under stable vehicle signal paths. A prototype on a resource-constrained edge gateway connected to an RR100 UGV demonstrates automated integration of a USB camera and an ultrasonic sensor. Across repeated integration cycles, the prototype reaches operational state in about 2s, shows no failed events, and keeps applications independent of hardware-specific interfaces. The results indicate that the introduction of AAS as an executable onboarding contract enables automated runtime deployment of sensor drivers in SDV environments.

papers.title: Model Discovery for Virtual Chaos Engineering with Incomplete Tracing: An eBPF Study
papers.summary: Model-based fault experiments can assess the consequences of component failures before intervening in a running application. Recent work on model discovery and graph simulation acquired operation models from application telemetry and used them for availability prediction. Applying this approach to operational legacy systems raises an acquisition problem: the required traces may be absent or incomplete, while introducing them can require changes across heterogeneous components. These systems continue to serve business operations during extended maintenance and modernization. External observation offers a possible route to model-based fault analysis before a tracing retrofit, but collecting telemetry does not by itself establish that an executable operation model can be obtained. We investigate this route using extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) observations and the existing graph-based modelling approach. A 108-case study varied application software development kit (SDK) tracing across absent, partial and full conditions in three public applications. Discovered dependencies were combined with declared operation requirements, deployment facts and scenario assumptions; model forecasts preceded independent execution checks. With SDK tracing disabled, the tested OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation path supported all seven operations in two applications across three repetitions. Forecasts agreed exactly in 17 of 21 operation-repetition groups; the maximum state-weighted discrepancy was 4.22 percentage points. Combining observed context links supported nine additional groups under partial tracing. The results establish an acquisition path for virtual fault experiments under the tested observation constraints and identify limits imposed by protocols, evidence association and operation semantics.

papers.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
papers.summary: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

papers.title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
papers.summary: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.

papers.title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
papers.summary: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

papers.title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
papers.summary: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

papers.title: Authenticating IoT Data on Ethereum after Pectra and Fusaka: A Cost Study of Signature Schemes, Batching and Anchoring for Agricultural Supply Chain Finance
papers.summary: Blockchain-based supply chain finance can turn the sensor-recorded production history of smallholder farms into verifiable credit evidence, but only if every record is authenticated and anchored at a cost that scales to large device fleets. Ethereum's 2025 Pectra and Fusaka upgrades changed this cost landscape: they added precompiles for BLS12-381 and P-256, repriced calldata and MODEXP, and capped transaction gas at $2^{24}$. We organize the authentication and anchoring of IoT records into three trust levels, from posting a Merkle root through a trusted aggregator to verifying every device signature on-chain, and implement four replay-protected signature designs: ECDSA over secp256k1 and P-256, BLS aggregate signatures with on-chain hash-to-curve, and a pseudonymous identity-based signature with batch verification. Measured as signed transactions under the rules before and after both upgrades, the upgrades mainly changed which designs are feasible, not their cost. Batching and Merkle anchoring cut the cost of ECDSA authentication sixfold, to 8,963 gas per record, and secp256k1 ECDSA remains the cheapest authenticated design: P-256 costs 1.6 times as much, the identity-based design 2.7 times and BLS aggregation 3.9 times, dominated by on-chain hashing to the curve. One transaction carries at most 1,754 ECDSA-authenticated records but only 411 BLS-aggregated ones. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, pairing-based signing takes 5.7 ms against 0.29 ms for ECDSA. Pairing-based designs pay off only when the application needs their additional properties, and the identity-based design adds key escrow at the key generation centre. The benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.

papers.title: Slice Isolation-as-a-Service: An Isolation Mechanism to Proactively Defend Cross-Slice Attacks in 5G-Advanced and Beyond
papers.summary: As cellular networks transition toward 5G-Advanced and Sixth Generation (6G) architectures, Network Slicing (NS) remains essential for multiplexing heterogeneous services over shared physical infrastructure. However, deploying critical Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communications (URLLC) alongside standard broadband introduces severe cross-slice vulnerabilities. The implicit assumption that logical slicing inherently guarantees security fails against data plane exploits, as shared User Plane Functions (UPFs) remain susceptible to resource starvation and protocol tunneling. To address this, we propose the Slice Isolation-as-a-Service framework, which treats topological data plane isolation as an on-demand, monetizable capability. We formulate the multi-UPF resource allocation problem as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model to strictly enforce physical and virtual isolation boundaries based on tenant security tiers, minimizing provisioning costs and end-to-end latency. To validate the framework, we engineered a novel containerized Fifth Generation (5G) testbed integrating Free5GC with Nokia Containerlab. Empirical evaluations under active volumetric flooding and the recently discovered GTP-in-GTP reflection attacks reveal that shared and Virtualized Network Function (VNF)-only isolation fail catastrophically, suffering up to 30% packet loss and complete bandwidth starvation. Our results prove that MINLP-driven strict physical isolation successfully neutralizes cross-slice injection and preserves 99.999% reliability for mission-critical slices, confirming our isolation framework as a crucial proactive defense for next-generation core networks.

papers.title: Training-Free Domain Generation for One-Shot Federated Learning with Server-Side Pre-trained Diffusion Models
papers.summary: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) has attracted increasing attention for its ability to substantially reduce communication overhead by limiting client-server interaction to a single communication round. Nevertheless, this limited interaction makes learning from heterogeneous client distributions challenging. Diffusion-based OSFL approaches seek to address this challenge by synthesizing data that approximate client distributions. However, existing diffusion-based approaches often impose substantial computational costs on clients and lack effective visual guidance to generate data aligned with client distributions. To address these limitations, we propose FedDoG, a training-free Domain Generation framework that leverages server-side pre-trained diffusion models to synthesize data aligned with client domains. FedDoG extracts compact domain representations using a frozen image encoder, substantially reducing client-side computational and communication costs. These representations are incorporated into the diffusion model through a pre-trained image-conditioning adapter, thereby providing explicit visual guidance for domain generation. To further improve the quality of synthetic data, FedDoG adapts the strength of visual conditioning according to domain concentration and filters generated samples based on class consistency and predictive entropy.
